summary_html: CPS **screens out** a report (no investigation) or closes as **unfounded** after minimal review. Federal law (CAPTA) conditions funding on operating screening criteria and recordkeeping; federal reviews (CFSR) assess decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — screening & intake system requirements  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal performance/quality review of state screening and responses

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: SRS (now DCF) owed the reporting children an actionable duty of care because 33 V.S.A. § 4915 imposes mandatory investigative acts for the protection of a particular class, and sovereign immunity did not bar the negligence suit.
key_cases.relevance: Screening a report out or leaving it unacted upon is not costless in Vermont: Sabia makes the failure to investigate a breach of an enforceable duty.
key_cases.quote: Accordingly, we conclude that SRS had a duty to protect plaintiffs under the circumstances of this case.

key_cases.holding: The substantiation and registry placement were reversed because they had to be supported by sufficient evidence known to DCF at the time of substantiation, and the petitioner's later admissions could not retroactively justify them.
key_cases.relevance: K.R. requires the record at the time of the decision to support the finding, which is the discipline that separates a sound screening call from a defective one.
key_cases.quote: However, after-acquired evidence cannot salvage a substantiation that was not supported by sufficient evidence in the first place.

key_cases.holding: The Human Services Board's reversal of a registry substantiation was itself reversed and remanded because the Board must apply the same substantiation standard DCF applies under its Policy No. 55 rather than a different standard of its own.
key_cases.relevance: The decision defines what a report must show before DCF may substantiate rather than close it out.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the Board should have used the standard embodied in Policy No. 55 and must do so on remand

key_cases.case_name: Tina Stocker v. State of Vermont
key_cases.holding: Judgment as a matter of law for the State was affirmed: the only non-discretionary DCF duty supporting a damages action is the 33 V.S.A. § 4915 duty to record a report and make an initial determination whether it is valid, assessment and investigation under §§ 4915a and 4915b are discretionary and within sovereign immunity, and plaintiffs could not show the recording failures proximately caused the children's continued abuse.
key_cases.relevance: Stocker is the modern Vermont limit on liability for screening decisions: DCF must record a report and decide whether it is valid, but its judgment whether the report meets the § 4912 definition of abuse is discretionary and immune.
key_cases.quote: any implied right of action against DCF based in this statutory scheme is limited to violations of mandatory duties pursuant to § 4915

timeline_requirements.deadline: 24 hours to document the safety determination and safety plan on the SDM Safety Assessment
timeline_requirements.starts_from: First in-person interview with the family
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Vermont DCF Family Services Policy 52 (effective 9/5/2024).

timeline_requirements.deadline: 60 days to conclude an investigation; 45 days to complete an assessment, or 60 days with written justification and supervisor approval
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Opening of the child safety intervention (the investigation or assessment track)
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in Vermont DCF Family Services Policy 52 (effective 9/5/2024); the policy allows an investigation to stay open past 60 days while a law enforcement or criminal case is unresolved, and an assessment extension may not exceed 60 days total (33 V.S.A. § 4915a(b)). Vermont sets no completion deadline for the investigation track by statute (33 V.S.A. § 4915b).
